_note: Checklists. 'source' says where the steps come from; full references are in docs/sources.md. Steps marked as written by the team are placeholders and are not medical advice.

RAD-01.title: Solar particle event in progress
RAD-01.why: The radiation dose rate has risen far above the usual background, which happens when a solar storm reaches the crew.
steps: Stop your current task and secure equipment
Move to the central stowage area, the most shielded part of the cabin
Stack storage bags around you to build the shelter, within one hour
Stay inside until the dose rate is back in the normal band, which can take up to 24 hours
Report any nausea or unusual tiredness
RAD-01.source: Adapted from NASA's Orion radiation shelter procedure (NASA, Scientists and Engineers Evaluate Orion Radiation Protection Plan).

HRT-01.title: Heart readings well above your baseline
HRT-01.why: Your heart rate or blood pressure is much higher than what is normal for you.
steps: Stop exercise or hard work and rest
Measure your blood pressure again after 10 minutes
Drink 250 ml of water
Press 'I need help' if you have chest pain, dizziness or trouble breathing
HRT-01.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice.

HRT-02.title: Blood pressure is low
HRT-02.why: Your blood pressure is below the level where dizziness or fainting become likely.
steps: Stop what you are doing and secure yourself
Drink 250 ml of water with electrolytes
Measure your blood pressure again after 10 minutes
Press 'I need help' if you feel faint or confused
HRT-02.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice.

GEN-01.title: You have a fever
GEN-01.why: Your body temperature is at fever level, which usually means your body is fighting an infection.
steps: Rest and stop exercise for today
Drink water regularly
Measure your temperature again in one hour
Keep your distance from crewmates where you can
Wait for the flight surgeon before taking any medication
GEN-01.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice. Trigger level from the CDC fever definition.

GEN-02.title: Blood sugar is low
GEN-02.why: Your blood sugar is below the level where shakiness, sweating and confusion can start.
steps: Eat or drink something sugary now
Rest for 15 minutes
Measure your blood sugar again
Eat a proper meal once it is back in range
GEN-02.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice. Trigger level from the American Diabetes Association.

GEN-03.title: Blood sugar is high
GEN-03.why: Your blood sugar is well above the normal range.
steps: Drink water
Note when and what you last ate
Measure your blood sugar again in one hour
Send the readings to the flight surgeon
GEN-03.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice.

GEN-04.title: Body temperature is low
GEN-04.why: Your body temperature is below the normal range.
steps: Put on extra layers
Move to a warmer part of the cabin
Have a warm drink
Measure your temperature again in 30 minutes
GEN-04.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice.

MND-01.title: Your sleep has dropped well below your usual
MND-01.why: You have been sleeping much less than usual, which affects attention, mood and safety.
steps: Move one task off today's schedule
Avoid caffeine for the rest of the day
Start winding down 30 minutes earlier tonight
Tell the flight surgeon if this continues for three nights
MND-01.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice. Supported by NASA's behavioral evidence report and Barger et al. (2014) on crew sleep.

BON-01.title: Exercise is well below your plan
BON-01.why: Without regular loading, bones and muscles weaken quickly in low gravity.
steps: Check which sessions were missed this week
Schedule a resistance session today
Report any pain or equipment problem that is stopping you
BON-01.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice. Supported by NASA: station crews exercise an average of two hours a day to counter bone loss.

EMG-BREATH.title: Trouble breathing
EMG-BREATH.why: Difficulty breathing is treated as the most urgent sign.
steps: Call a crewmate to stay with you now
Stop all activity and stay upright
Loosen anything tight around your neck and chest
Check the cabin air alarms and move to another module if any are active
Have the crewmate get the medical kit and oxygen
EMG-BREATH.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice.

EMG-CHEST.title: Chest pain or pressure
EMG-CHEST.why: Chest pain can come from the heart and must not be waited out.
steps: Call a crewmate to stay with you now
Stop all activity and rest
Have the crewmate measure your heart rate and blood pressure
Have the crewmate get the medical kit
Do not exercise until the flight surgeon replies
EMG-CHEST.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice.

EMG-BLEED.title: Bleeding that will not stop
EMG-BLEED.why: Continued bleeding needs direct pressure straight away.
steps: Press firmly on the wound with a clean dressing
Call a crewmate to help
Keep pressing without lifting to look for 10 minutes
Add another dressing on top if blood soaks through
Have the crewmate get the medical kit
EMG-BLEED.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice.

EMG-NEURO.title: Fainting or confusion
EMG-NEURO.why: Fainting or confusion can mean the brain is not getting what it needs.
steps: Call a crewmate to stay with you now
Secure yourself so you cannot drift or fall
Have the crewmate check your blood sugar, heart rate and blood pressure
Do not operate equipment
Tell the crewmate if your speech, vision or strength changes
EMG-NEURO.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice.

EMG-HEAD.title: Head pain
EMG-HEAD.why: Headaches are common in spaceflight but a severe or sudden one needs checking.
steps: Stop your task and rest in a dimmer area
Drink 250 ml of water
Check the cabin air readings
Tell a crewmate if your vision changes or the pain is the worst you have had
Rate the pain again in 30 minutes
EMG-HEAD.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice.

EMG-BACK.title: Back or neck pain
EMG-BACK.why: The spine lengthens in low gravity, which often causes back pain, but injuries need to be ruled out.
steps: Stop lifting, pulling or exercise
Find the position that hurts least and rest in it
Tell a crewmate if you have numbness or weakness in an arm or leg
Rate the pain again in 30 minutes
EMG-BACK.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice.

EMG-ABDO.title: Abdominal pain
EMG-ABDO.why: Abdominal pain has many causes and some are serious.
steps: Stop eating and exercise for now
Rest in the position that hurts least
Measure your temperature
Tell a crewmate if the pain is getting worse or you are vomiting
Rate the pain again in 30 minutes
EMG-ABDO.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice.

EMG-LIMB.title: Arm or leg injury
EMG-LIMB.why: A hurt limb should be rested and checked before it is used again.
steps: Stop using the limb
Check that you can move and feel your fingers or toes
Apply a cold pack for 15 minutes
Have a crewmate support it with a splint or wrap if it hurts to move
Rate the pain again in 30 minutes
EMG-LIMB.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice.

EMG-GEN.title: Feeling unwell
EMG-GEN.why: No specific danger sign was reported, so the first step is to get checked.
steps: Stop your current task
Tell a crewmate how you feel
Measure your temperature, heart rate and blood pressure
Drink water and rest
Press 'I need help' again if anything gets worse
EMG-GEN.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice.

LNG-01.title: Blood oxygen is low
LNG-01.why: Your blood is carrying less oxygen than it should.
steps: Stop what you are doing and rest
Take slow, deep breaths for two minutes
Check the cabin air alarms and move to another module if any are active
Measure your blood oxygen again after five minutes
Press 'I need help' if you feel short of breath
LNG-01.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice.

GEN-05.title: You have not had enough to drink
GEN-05.why: Your water intake today is well below the daily plan.
steps: Drink 250 ml of water now
Drink another 250 ml each hour until you reach 2 litres
Note the colour of your urine at your next visit
Tell the flight surgeon if you feel dizzy or have a headache
GEN-05.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice.

EMG-CUT.title: Cut or scratch
EMG-CUT.why: Small wounds heal more slowly in space, so cleaning and covering them matters.
steps: Put on gloves from the medical kit
Press on the wound with clean gauze until bleeding stops
Clean around it with an antiseptic wipe
Cover it with a sterile dressing
Tell the crew medical officer if anything is stuck in it or it will not close
EMG-CUT.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice.

EMG-BRUISE.title: Bruise or impact
EMG-BRUISE.why: A hard knock can hide a deeper injury, so check movement and swelling.
steps: Stop using the injured area
Apply a cold pack for 15 minutes
Check that you can move it and feel your fingers or toes
Tell the crew medical officer if you cannot move it or the swelling keeps growing
Rate the pain again in 30 minutes
EMG-BRUISE.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice.

EMG-BURN.title: Burn
EMG-BURN.why: Burns need cooling quickly and protection from infection.
steps: Move away from what caused the burn
Cool the burn with a cool, wet cloth for 10 minutes
Remove anything tight near the burn before it swells
Cover it loosely with a sterile dressing
Do not break blisters; tell the crew medical officer if it is blistered, large, chemical or electrical
EMG-BURN.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice.

EMG-ILL.title: Feeling ill
EMG-ILL.why: In a closed cabin an illness can spread, so it is checked early.
steps: Stop your current task and rest
Measure your temperature, heart rate and blood oxygen
Drink water in small sips
Keep your distance from crewmates where you can
Press 'I need help' again if you get worse
EMG-ILL.source: Steps written by the team. Not medical advice.
